newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian, world rice price gap seen concern.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian, world rice price gap seen concern.

text.p: Australian ricegrowers should have every reason to celebrate as world rice prices ride high and Australia heads for a record rice crop of 1.45 million tonnes in 1996/97.
But gloom is deepening as world markets boom.

Chicago's strong rice futures market was further boosted earlier this week by the USDA's cut on Wednesday of forecast U.S. ending rice stocks to 24.3 million cwt from 25.3 million cwt. The market is underpinned by tight supplies and strong export markets.
Flat returns for Australian growers, however, are producing discontent among growers and brokers and raising questions about the transparency of the Australian market.
The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) in its recent Outlook papers forecast grower returns for 1996/97 will edge back to A$192 a tonne for paddy from A$207.
Milling costs about one-third of the price of milled rice, producing a milled price equivalent of about A$288 on the forecast grower return of A$192 for paddy.
In U.S. dollar terms, this is equivalent to about $220 a tonne, compared with world prices of more than $300 milled.

ABARE rice analyst Max Foster told Reuters the Australian rice industry was looking at an "absolutely bin-bursting harvest", far ahead of the previous record of 1.14 million tonnes in 1994/95 (harvest May-June).
This was likely to stretch Australia's logistical system and could be exerting some downward pressure on prices, he said.
But the gap between rising world prices and flat domestic returns in Australia raised questions about the marketing margin, one trade source, who requested anonymity, said.

Michael Hedditch, executive director of the Ricegrowers Association of Australia, told Reuters that Australian rice was not priced off Chicago futures, which he described as an unreliable and thin market.
World traded rice against total production was also thin and did not provide a reliable guide to market reality, he said.
Selling the 1997 crop was still in progress, although it had been totally committed with forecast returns to growers about A$200 a tonne, he said.
Growers were being told not to budget for prices above the the 1996 return of A$207, he said.

Hedditch said the difference between Asian rice prices and Australian returns was due to local prices being based on paddy rice at the farm gate and Asian prices being based on a milled, packaged product.

A commodities broker with the Sydney Futures Exchange, who asked that he not be identified, disagreed. The Rice Marketing Board's single desk monopoly export rights robbed the market of transparency, he said.
Australia's rice monopoly had been caught unaware by the world rice price surge after having sold the crop at comparatively low prices, he said.
Another market source also said Australia's rice price was likely to have been placed under pressure by difficulties in marketing a bumper crop.
While Chicago may reflect domestic U.S. conditions, both Australia and the U.S. produced Japonica types of rice.

This suggested that Australia's exports of about 800,000 tonnes of milled rice, about five percent of total world traded rice of about 18 million tonnes, should more closely follow Chicago futures prices, the source said.
Difficulties in accessing the Japanese market could also help explain Australia's low domestic price return, he said.

Australia's quoted rice export prices have been rising with the trend in world prices, with the price of whole long grained milled or semi-milled rice reaching A$688 a tonne in December from the September price of A$635.
But Australian grower returns were close to A$100 a tonne below world market prices, while Chicago futures prices were much closer to world market prices, the futures broker said.
Chicago March futures closed at US$12.14 a cwt, equal to US$242.80 a long ton, on Thursday.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
